notes.front: Under the Exchange Act, who is an associated person of a member?
notes.back: Any partner, officer, director or branch manager of the member, anyone controlling, controlled by or under common control with it, or any employee.
notes.explanation: People in a similar status or performing similar functions under other titles are included too.
notes.example: Like everyone on a company’s board or payroll, plus those who control it, but for a broker-dealer that is a member.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. 78c (Exchange Act s. 3), subsection (a), paragraph (21)
notes.evidence: means any partner, officer, director, or branch manager of such member (or any person occupying a similar status or performing similar functions), any person directly or indirectly controlling, controlled by, or under common control with such member, or any employee of such member.

notes.front: Under FINRA’s registration rules, which associated persons are representatives who must register (registered representatives)?
notes.back: Associated persons engaged in the member’s investment banking or securities business, for example in supervision, solicitation or conducting business in securities.
notes.explanation: Training people for those functions also counts, and an assistant officer who is not a principal can be a representative.
notes.example: Like a salesperson who opens accounts and takes orders for a broker-dealer’s clients.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2017-07046 (2017-04-10), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed consolidated registration rules, section 14, “Definition of Representative”
notes.evidence: defines the term ``representative'' as an associated person, including an assistant officer other than a principal, who is engaged in the investment banking or securities business for the member, such as supervision, solicitation, conduct of business in securities or the training of persons associated with a member for any of these functions.

notes.front: What is the Securities Industry Essentials (SIE) examination?
notes.back: FINRA’s general knowledge examination, which new representative-level applicants take together with a specialised exam for their particular role.
notes.explanation: The SIE covers general securities knowledge; the second, tailored exam covers the knowledge needed for the specific registered role.
notes.example: Like a common first-year course every engineering student takes before specialising in civil, mechanical or electrical engineering.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2018-01678 (2018-01-30), SEC notice of FINRA’s filing on the new SIE examination, “Purpose”
notes.evidence: all new representative-level applicants will be required to take a general knowledge examination (the SIE) and a tailored, specialized knowledge examination (a revised representative-level qualification examination) for their particular registered role.

notes.front: What is a statutory disqualification?
notes.back: An Exchange Act section 3(a)(39) status, triggered by events such as SRO expulsions, bars or certain convictions, affecting membership in or association with a member.
notes.explanation: The definition applies to membership or participation in a self-regulatory organisation, or association with one of its members, and lists the events that trigger it.
notes.example: Like a licensing rule that flags anyone with certain past bans or convictions before they can work in the industry.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. 78c (Exchange Act s. 3), subsection (a), paragraph (39)
notes.evidence: A person is subject to a "statutory disqualification" with respect to membership or participation in, or association with a member of, a self-regulatory organization, if such person-

notes.front: What is continuing education (CE) for registered persons, and what are its two parts?
notes.back: Ongoing education registered persons must complete, made up of a Regulatory Element and a Firm Element.
notes.explanation: For FINRA members the CE Program is codified in FINRA Rule 1240.
notes.example: Like the yearly training doctors or accountants must complete to keep practising, after their initial qualifying exams.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2021-13286 (2021-06-24), SEC notice of proposed amendments to FINRA Rules 1210 and 1240, “Purpose”, (i) Background
notes.evidence: The continuing education program for registered persons of broker- dealers (``CE Program'') currently requires registered persons to complete continuing education consisting of a Regulatory Element and a Firm Element.

notes.front: What is the Regulatory Element of CE, and when must it be completed?
notes.back: The part of CE every registered person must complete annually, by 31 December.
notes.explanation: Firms may require their registered persons to complete it earlier than 31 December, for example to line it up with other training.
notes.example: Like an annual refresher, set by the licensing body, that every licence holder must finish by the end of the year.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2021-20818 (2021-09-27), SEC order approving amendments to FINRA Rules 1210 and 1240, section II.B
notes.evidence: require registered persons to complete the Regulatory Element of the CE Program annually by December 31. Firms, however, would have the flexibility to require their registered persons to complete the Regulatory Element sooner than December 31
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: What is the Firm Element of CE?
notes.back: An annual training programme each firm develops and administers for its registered persons.
notes.explanation: At a minimum it includes ethics and professional responsibility, plus training on the products, services and strategies the member offers.
notes.example: Like a hospital’s own yearly training on its equipment and procedures, on top of a doctor’s national licence requirements.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2021-20818 (2021-09-27), SEC order approving amendments to FINRA Rules 1210 and 1240, section II.C
notes.evidence: Currently, Rule 1240(b) requires a firm to develop and administer an annual Firm Element training program for its covered registered persons.\29\ The Firm Element must, at a minimum, include training in ethics and professional responsibility

notes.front: What is Form U4?
notes.back: The Uniform Application for Securities Industry Registration or Transfer: the uniform form used to register an individual and disclose required information.
notes.explanation: It is one of the Uniform Forms, alongside Form BD for firms and a separate termination form, and disclosures on it have a 30-calendar-day reporting deadline.
notes.example: Like a professional licence application that also records your work, criminal and disciplinary history and must be kept up to date.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2010-19505 (2010-08-09), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed Rule 4530 (Reporting Requirements), “Reporting Deadline”
notes.evidence: The proposed 30-calendar-day reporting deadline also is consistent with the reporting deadline for disclosing information on the Forms BD (Uniform Application for Broker-Dealer Registration), U4 (Uniform Application for Securities Industry Registration or Transfer) and U5 (Uniform Termination Notice for Securities Industry Registration)

notes.front: What is Form U5?
notes.back: The Uniform Termination Notice for Securities Industry Registration: the form that ends an individual’s registration with a firm.
notes.explanation: Like Form U4 it is one of the Uniform Forms, and disclosures on it share the 30-calendar-day reporting deadline.
notes.example: Like an employer’s formal notice to a licensing body that someone has left and no longer holds a licence through that firm.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2010-19505 (2010-08-09), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed Rule 4530 (Reporting Requirements), “Reporting Deadline”
notes.evidence: The proposed 30-calendar-day reporting deadline also is consistent with the reporting deadline for disclosing information on the Forms BD (Uniform Application for Broker-Dealer Registration), U4 (Uniform Application for Securities Industry Registration or Transfer) and U5 (Uniform Termination Notice for Securities Industry Registration)

notes.front: For a broker-dealer’s records, what is a written customer complaint, and what must the record of it show?
notes.back: A customer’s written complaint concerning an associated person; the record shows who complained, when, its nature and its disposition.
notes.explanation: The record also gives the complainant’s address and account number and names any other associated person identified in the complaint.
notes.example: Like a client’s letter saying their adviser sold them a product they never agreed to buy.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17a-3 (Rule 17a-3), paragraph (a), paragraph (a)(18)
notes.evidence: each written customer complaint received by the member, broker or dealer concerning that associated person. The record must include the complainant's name, address, and account number; the date the complaint was received; the name of any other associated person identified in the complaint; a description of the nature of the complaint; and the disposition of the complaint.

notes.front: What is a red flag in the conduct of a broker?
notes.back: A warning sign of possible misconduct; for churning, the SEC lists unauthorised trading, frequent trading and excessive fees.
notes.explanation: A red flag is a reason to look closer, not proof: the SEC says red flags of excessive trading “may include” these.
notes.example: Like a smoke alarm: not proof of fire, but a reason to check straight away.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Churning”
notes.evidence: Red flags of excessive trading may include: - Unauthorized Trading – Be alarmed if you become aware of trades in your account that you did not authorize your broker to make. - Frequent Trading – Be wary of frequent in-and-out purchases and sales of securities that don’t seem consistent with your investment goals and risk tolerance. - Excessive Fees

notes.front: What is an outside business activity (OBA) under FINRA Rule 3270?
notes.back: Business activity outside the scope of a registered person’s relationship with the firm, such as working for, or being paid by, another person.
notes.explanation: The rule covers being another person’s employee, independent contractor, sole proprietor, officer, director or partner, or being paid or expecting pay from another person.
notes.example: Like a representative who also runs a paid bookkeeping business at weekends.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2026-19126 (2026-09-18), SEC order approving FINRA Rule 3290 (Outside Activities Requirements), section II.A.1
notes.evidence: Subject to several exemptions, FINRA Rule 3270 prohibits a registered person from being an employee, independent contractor, sole proprietor, officer, director or partner of another person, or being compensated, or having the reasonable expectation of compensation, by any other person as a result of any business activity outside the scope of the relationship with his or her member firm
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rules 3270 and 3280 in force; replacement Rule 3290 approved, effective date not set

notes.front: What is a private securities transaction (PST) under FINRA Rule 3280?
notes.back: Any securities transaction outside the regular course or scope of an associated person’s employment with the firm, subject to listed exclusions.
notes.explanation: Exclusions include transactions among immediate family members with no selling compensation, and personal transactions in investment company and variable annuity securities.
notes.example: Like a representative selling shares in a friend’s start-up to people she knows, without the deal going through her firm.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2026-19126 (2026-09-18), SEC order approving FINRA Rule 3290 (Outside Activities Requirements), footnote 13
notes.evidence: FINRA Rule 3280(e)(1) defines a PST as any securities transaction outside the regular course or scope of an associated person's employment with a member, excluding:
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rules 3270 and 3280 in force; replacement Rule 3290 approved, effective date not set

notes.front: What is selling compensation under FINRA Rule 3280?
notes.back: Any compensation paid directly or indirectly, from whatever source, in connection with or as a result of the purchase or sale of a security.
notes.explanation: The definition is deliberately wide: the source of the payment and whether it is direct or indirect do not matter.
notes.example: Like a finder’s fee or a share of the profits received for arranging someone’s investment.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2026-19126 (2026-09-18), SEC order approving FINRA Rule 3290 (Outside Activities Requirements), footnote 13
notes.evidence: FINRA Rule 3280(e)(2) defines ``selling compensation'' as any compensation paid directly or indirectly from whatever source in connection with, or as a result of, the purchase or sale of a security.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rules 3270 and 3280 in force; replacement Rule 3290 approved, effective date not set

notes.front: What do FINRA’s non-cash compensation rules restrict?
notes.back: Paying or receiving non-cash compensation in connection with the sale and distribution of the securities those rules govern.
notes.explanation: The rules are FINRA Rules 2310, 2320, 2341 and 5110, covering direct participation programmes, variable insurance contracts, investment company securities and underwriting terms.
notes.example: Like a fund company offering a representative a free holiday, rather than cash, in connection with selling its funds.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2020-06187 (2020-03-25), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed suitability and non-cash compensation changes, “Non-Cash Compensation”
notes.evidence: each includes provisions restricting the payment and receipt of non-cash compensation in connection with the sale and distribution of securities governed by those rules.

notes.front: In FINRA’s non-cash compensation rules, what kind of business entertainment is allowed?
notes.back: An occasional meal, a ticket to a sporting event or the theatre, or comparable entertainment that raises no question of propriety.
notes.explanation: It must also not be preconditioned on achieving a sales target.
notes.example: Like taking a client’s staff to dinner once after a long meeting.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2020-06187 (2020-03-25), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed suitability and non-cash compensation changes, “Non-Cash Compensation”
notes.evidence: An occasional meal, a ticket to a sporting event or the theater, or other comparable entertainment that does not raise any question of propriety and is not preconditioned on the achievement of a sales target;

notes.front: What is BrokerCheck?
notes.back: A free tool on FINRA’s website designed to help investors make informed choices about associated persons and broker-dealer firms.
notes.explanation: It covers the people and firms with which investors do or may do business.
notes.example: Like a public register where you can look up whether a doctor is licensed and has any disciplinary history.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2024-14974 (2024-07-09), SEC notice of amendments to FINRA Rule 8312 (BrokerCheck Disclosure), “FINRA’s BrokerCheck Tool”
notes.evidence: BrokerCheck is a free tool available on FINRA's website that is designed to help investors make informed choices about the associated persons and broker-dealer firms with which they conduct or may conduct business.

notes.front: What is arbitration?
notes.back: Resolving a dispute outside the courts: the parties agree to have one or more arbitrators hear it and to be bound by their decision.
notes.explanation: It is a form of alternative dispute resolution; most broker-dealer customer account agreements contain arbitration clauses.
notes.example: Like asking an agreed referee to settle a disagreement and accepting the ruling, instead of going to court.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Arbitration and Mediation”
notes.evidence: Arbitration, a form of alternative dispute resolution, is a technique for the resolution of disputes outside the court system. In arbitration, the parties agree to have their dispute heard by one or more arbitrators and agree to be bound by their decision.

notes.front: What are the FINRA By-Laws?
notes.back: FINRA’s governing provisions, separate from the Rules of FINRA and arranged in articles, such as Article III on who may associate with a member.
notes.explanation: FINRA filings distinguish the By-Laws, the Schedules to the By-Laws and the Rules of FINRA; rules and orders then cite By-Law articles such as Article III or Article V.
notes.example: Like a club’s constitution, which sits alongside its day-to-day rules.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2018-01678 (2018-01-30), SEC notice of FINRA’s filing on the new SIE examination, section I
notes.evidence: FINRA is not proposing any textual changes to the By-Laws, Schedules to the By-Laws or Rules of FINRA.

notes.front: Is every associated person required to register with FINRA?
notes.back: No: associated persons whose functions are solely and exclusively clerical or ministerial are exempt from registration.
notes.explanation: Registration follows function: someone engaged in the securities business as a representative registers, while purely clerical or ministerial staff do not have to.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2017-07046 (2017-04-10), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed consolidated registration rules, section N
notes.evidence: both the NASD rules and the Incorporated NYSE rules provide an exemption from registration for associated persons whose functions are solely and exclusively clerical or ministerial.

notes.front: Under FINRA Rule 1210.02, may an associated person who does not need a registration still obtain one?
notes.back: Yes: any associated person may obtain and maintain any registration the member permits.
notes.explanation: For example, someone working solely in a clerical or administrative role could hold a General Securities Representative registration.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2017-07046 (2017-04-10), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed consolidated registration rules, section C, “Permissive Registrations”
notes.evidence: proposed FINRA Rule 1210.02 allows any associated person to obtain and maintain any registration permitted by the member.

notes.front: Which of these associated persons must register as a representative: (1) a receptionist who only answers phones and files papers; (2) an employee who solicits new brokerage clients?
notes.back: Only the employee who solicits clients; the receptionist’s functions are clerical or ministerial.
notes.choices:
A) Only the employee who solicits clients
B) Both
C) Neither, as both are employees
notes.choicesExplained: B: purely clerical or ministerial staff are exempt. C: soliciting clients is securities business that requires registration.
notes.explanation: Solicitation is a representative function; filing and answering phones is clerical or ministerial.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2017-07046 (2017-04-10), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed consolidated registration rules, section N
notes.evidence: both the NASD rules and the Incorporated NYSE rules provide an exemption from registration for associated persons whose functions are solely and exclusively clerical or ministerial.

notes.front: Does passing the SIE alone qualify someone for registration with FINRA?
notes.back: No: they must also be associated with a firm, pass the appropriate representative or principal exam and meet the other registration requirements.
notes.explanation: The SIE is one of two exams for new representatives; the second is tailored to the role at the firm they join.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2018-01678 (2018-01-30), SEC notice of FINRA’s filing on the new SIE examination, “Purpose”
notes.evidence: passing the SIE examination alone will not qualify an individual for registration with FINRA. To be eligible for registration, an individual must also be associated with a firm, pass an appropriate qualification examination for representative or principal and satisfy the other requirements relating to the registration process.

notes.front: Must someone be associated with a FINRA member firm to take the SIE?
notes.back: No: individuals need not be associated with a member to be eligible to take it.
notes.explanation: Association with a firm becomes necessary only for registration, not for sitting the SIE.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2018-01678 (2018-01-30), SEC notice of FINRA’s filing on the new SIE examination, “Purpose”
notes.evidence: Individuals are not required to be associated with a FINRA [[Page 4376]] member to be eligible to take the SIE examination.

notes.front: A university student passes the SIE but has no job at a broker-dealer. Can she now register as a representative?
notes.back: No: she must associate with a firm and pass a representative-level exam, such as the Series 7, before registering.
notes.choices:
A) No
B) Yes, the SIE is a full registration
C) Yes, once she applies to FINRA directly
notes.choicesExplained: B: the SIE alone does not qualify anyone for registration. C: an individual must be associated with a firm, which files the registration.
notes.explanation: Registration needs association with a firm plus the appropriate qualification exam, on top of the SIE.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2018-01678 (2018-01-30), SEC notice of FINRA’s filing on the new SIE examination, “Purpose”
notes.evidence: new applicants seeking to register as representatives must pass the SIE examination and a revised representative-level qualification examination, such as the revised General Securities Representative (Series 7) examination, appropriate to their job functions at the firm with which they are associating

notes.front: How long is a passing SIE result valid?
notes.back: Four years from the date it is passed.
notes.explanation: Within that time the person can pass a representative-level exam and register without retaking the SIE.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2017-07046 (2017-04-10), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed consolidated registration rules, section I, “Lapse of Registration and Expiration of SIE”
notes.evidence: FINRA is proposing that a passing result on the SIE be valid for four years.

notes.front: Someone passed the SIE three years ago while at university and has just joined a broker-dealer. Must she retake the SIE before registering?
notes.back: No: the result is still within its four years; she needs to pass a representative-level exam.
notes.choices:
A) No
B) Yes, the SIE lasts only two years
C) Yes, because she was not associated when she passed it
notes.choicesExplained: B: two years is the lapse period for representative and principal registrations, not the SIE. C: someone not associated when passing still has four years.
notes.explanation: A person who was not associated when passing the SIE has up to four years to associate with a firm, pass a representative exam and register.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2017-07046 (2017-04-10), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed consolidated registration rules, section I, “Lapse of Registration and Expiration of SIE”
notes.evidence: an individual who passes the SIE and is not an associated person at the time would have up to four years from the date he or she passes the SIE to become an associated person of a firm and pass a representative- level examination

notes.front: How is the two-year lapse period for a terminated registration measured?
notes.back: From the termination date on the individual’s Form U5 to the date FINRA receives a new application.
notes.explanation: If two or more years pass, the person must pass the qualification exam for the registration category again.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2017-07046 (2017-04-10), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed consolidated registration rules, section I, “Lapse of Registration and Expiration of SIE”
notes.evidence: The two years are calculated from the termination date stated on the individual's Form U5 (Uniform Termination Notice for Securities Industry Registration) and the date FINRA receives a new application for registration.

notes.front: How does the expiry of an SIE result differ from the lapse of a representative registration?
notes.back: An SIE pass lasts four years; representative and principal registrations lapse after two years out of the industry.
notes.explanation: The four-year period applies only to the SIE, not to representative- and principal-level registrations.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2017-07046 (2017-04-10), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed consolidated registration rules, section I, “Lapse of Registration and Expiration of SIE”
notes.evidence: the four-year expiration period in the proposed rule change extends only to the SIE, and not the representative- and principal-level registrations. The representative- and principal-level registrations would continue to be subject to a two-year expiration period

notes.front: Under Rule 1240 as amended, how can an eligible person who terminates a registration keep the qualification beyond two years?
notes.back: By electing to maintain it through continuing education, for up to five years.
notes.explanation: Conditions apply: for example, the person must have held the registration for at least a year before terminating and must complete all prescribed CE each year.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2021-20818 (2021-09-27), SEC order approving amendments to FINRA Rules 1210 and 1240, section II.D
notes.evidence: to provide eligible individuals who terminate any of their representative or principal registrations the option of maintaining their qualification for any of the terminated registrations for up to five years by completing continuing education.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: A General Securities Representative left the industry three years ago and did not elect to maintain her qualification. She now rejoins a firm. What must she do?
notes.back: Pass the representative exam again; her registration has lapsed, but her SIE still counts because she left less than four years ago.
notes.choices:
A) Retake the representative exam only
B) Nothing: registrations never lapse
C) Retake both the SIE and the representative exam
notes.choicesExplained: B: registrations lapse after two years out. C: someone who left holding a representative registration has four years before needing the SIE again.
notes.explanation: Three years exceeds the two-year lapse period, but a departing representative has up to four years to return without retaking the SIE.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2017-07046 (2017-04-10), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed consolidated registration rules, section I, “Lapse of Registration and Expiration of SIE”
notes.evidence: an individual holding a representative-level registration who leaves the industry after the effective date of the proposed rule change would have up to four years to reassociate with a firm and register as a representative without having to retake the SIE.

notes.front: Under section 3(a)(39)(F), how recent must a felony conviction be to make someone subject to a statutory disqualification?
notes.back: Within ten years of the date the application for membership or association is filed.
notes.explanation: The same subparagraph also covers convictions for the offences listed in section 15(b)(4)(B).
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. 78c (Exchange Act s. 3), subsection (a), paragraph (39)(F)
notes.evidence: has been convicted of any offense specified in subparagraph (B) of such paragraph (4) or any other felony within ten years of the date of the filing of an application for membership or participation in, or to become associated with a member of, such self-regulatory organization

notes.front: Under section 3(a)(39)(A), which regulatory history makes someone subject to a statutory disqualification?
notes.back: Being expelled or suspended from, or barred or suspended from association with a member of, a self-regulatory organisation, among other bodies.
notes.explanation: The list also includes foreign equivalents, foreign exchanges and certain futures bodies.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. 78c (Exchange Act s. 3), subsection (a), paragraph (39)(A)
notes.evidence: has been and is expelled or suspended from membership or participation in, or barred or suspended from being associated with a member of, any self-regulatory organization

notes.front: Under section 3(a)(39)(F), what filing misconduct can itself cause a statutory disqualification?
notes.back: Wilfully making a materially false or misleading statement, or omitting a required material fact, in an application, report or proceeding with an SRO.
notes.explanation: It covers applications to become associated with a member as well as reports filed with a self-regulatory organisation.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. 78c (Exchange Act s. 3), subsection (a), paragraph (39)(F)
notes.evidence: report required to be filed with a self-regulatory organization, or proceeding before a self-regulatory organization, any statement which was at the time, and in the light of the circumstances under which it was made, false or misleading with respect to any material fact

notes.front: An applicant was convicted of a felony unrelated to finance six years ago. Does the conviction make him subject to a statutory disqualification?
notes.back: Yes: section 3(a)(39)(F) covers any felony within ten years of the application.
notes.choices:
A) Yes
B) No, because it is unrelated to finance
C) No, because it was more than five years ago
notes.choicesExplained: B: the paragraph reaches “any other felony”, not only financial crimes. C: the look-back period is ten years.
notes.explanation: Six years is inside the ten-year window, and the paragraph is not limited to financial felonies.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. 78c (Exchange Act s. 3), subsection (a), paragraph (39)(F)
notes.evidence: has been convicted of any offense specified in subparagraph (B) of such paragraph (4) or any other felony within ten years of the date of the filing of an application for membership or participation in, or to become associated with a member of, such self-regulatory organization

notes.front: Besides Exchange Act sections 3(a)(39) and 15(b)(4), where are the eligibility conditions for association with a FINRA member set out?
notes.back: In Article III of the FINRA By-Laws.
notes.explanation: Meeting those conditions is required in addition to any requalification by examination.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2021-13286 (2021-06-24), SEC notice of proposed amendments to FINRA Rules 1210 and 1240, footnote to the CE programme example
notes.evidence: This would be in addition to satisfying the eligibility conditions for association with a FINRA member firm. See Exchange Act Sections 3(a)(39) and 15(b)(4) and Article III of the FINRA By-Laws.

notes.front: Under FINRA Rule 3110(e), what must a member ascertain by investigation before applying to register an applicant?
notes.back: The applicant’s good character, business reputation, qualifications and experience.
notes.explanation: The investigation must come before the member applies to register the person and before it represents on the application that it has investigated.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2014-30902 (2015-01-06), SEC order approving FINRA Rule 3110(e), section III
notes.evidence: each member ascertain by investigation the good character, business reputation, qualifications and experience of an applicant before the member applies to register that applicant with FINRA and before making a representation to that effect on the application for registration.

notes.front: If an applicant was registered before, whose form must the hiring firm review under Rule 3110(e), and within what time?
notes.back: The applicant’s most recent Form U5, including amendments, within 60 days of filing the applicant’s Form U4.
notes.explanation: If it cannot review the Form U5, the firm must show it made reasonable efforts to do so.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2014-30902 (2015-01-06), SEC order approving FINRA Rule 3110(e), section III
notes.evidence: requires that a firm review a copy of the applicant's most recent Form U5, including any amendments, within 60 days of the filing date of the applicant's Form U4.

notes.front: By when must a firm complete a search of reasonably available public records to verify an applicant’s initial or transfer Form U4?
notes.back: No later than 30 calendar days after the Form U4 is filed with FINRA.
notes.explanation: The requirement applies to initial and transfer Forms U4, not to later amendments.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2014-30902 (2015-01-06), SEC order approving FINRA Rule 3110(e), section II
notes.evidence: The requirement to conduct a public records search must be satisfied no later than 30 calendar days after the initial or transfer Form U4 is filed with FINRA.

notes.front: A firm wants to register a representative who worked at another member until last month. What must the firm review as part of its background investigation?
notes.back: A copy of her most recent Form U5, including amendments, within 60 days of filing her Form U4.
notes.choices:
A) Her most recent Form U5
B) Only her references and employment history
C) Nothing, since she was registered before
notes.choicesExplained: B: the rule specifically requires review of the prior Form U5 where the applicant was registered before. C: prior registration is what triggers the Form U5 review.
notes.explanation: Because she was previously registered, Rule 3110(e) requires the firm to review her latest Form U5.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2014-30902 (2015-01-06), SEC order approving FINRA Rule 3110(e), section III
notes.evidence: if an applicant has been previously registered with FINRA or another self-regulatory organization, proposed FINRA Rule 3110(e) requires that a firm review a copy of the applicant's most recent Form U5

notes.front: Under SEC Rule 17f-2, whose fingerprints must a broker or dealer obtain, and to whom are they submitted?
notes.back: Those of each partner, director, officer and employee, unless exempt; they go to the Attorney General of the United States or a designee.
notes.explanation: The same duty applies to exchange members, registered transfer agents and registered clearing agencies.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17f-2 (Rule 17f-2), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: every member of a national securities exchange, broker, dealer, registered transfer agent and registered clearing agency shall require that each of its partners, directors, officers and employees be fingerprinted and shall submit, or cause to be submitted, the fingerprints of such persons to the Attorney General of the United States or its designee

notes.front: Under Rule 17f-2, what three conditions exempt a broker-dealer’s employee from fingerprinting?
notes.back: Not selling securities; no regular access to securities, money or the original records; and no direct supervision of people who do.
notes.explanation: The firm may claim the exemption only if the rule’s notice requirements are also met.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17f-2 (Rule 17f-2), paragraph (a)(1)(i)
notes.evidence: (A) Is not engaged in the sale of securities; (B) Does not regularly have access to the keeping, handling or processing of ( 1 ) securities, ( 2 ) monies, or ( 3 ) the original books and records relating to the securities or the monies; and (C) Does not have direct supervisory responsibility over persons engaged in the activities

notes.front: A broker-dealer hires a cashier who will handle customer cheques every day but will not sell securities. Can the firm claim the Rule 17f-2 exemption for her?
notes.back: No: she regularly handles money, so she must be fingerprinted.
notes.choices:
A) No
B) Yes, because she does not sell securities
C) Yes, because she is not registered
notes.choicesExplained: B: not selling is only one of the three conditions; regular handling of money fails another. C: registration status is not one of the conditions.
notes.explanation: The exemption needs all three conditions, and regular access to handling money rules it out.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17f-2 (Rule 17f-2), paragraph (a)(1)(i)
notes.evidence: (B) Does not regularly have access to the keeping, handling or processing of ( 1 ) securities, ( 2 ) monies, or ( 3 ) the original books and records relating to the securities or the monies;

notes.front: Under Rule 15b7-1, what do the qualification standards a person must meet before effecting transactions include?
notes.back: Among others, submitting and maintaining all required forms, paying all required fees and passing any required examinations.
notes.explanation: A broker-dealer may not effect or induce securities transactions through a natural person who has not met them.
notes.evidence: standards of training, experience, competence, and other qualification standards (including but not limited to submitting and maintaining all required forms, paying all required fees, and passing any required examinations)

notes.front: Besides requiring many offerings to be registered, whom do state blue-sky laws license?
notes.back: Brokerage firms, their brokers and investment adviser representatives.
notes.explanation: Every state has its own securities laws on top of the federal ones, designed to protect investors against fraudulent sales practices.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Blue Sky Laws”
notes.evidence: The laws also license brokerage firms, their brokers, and investment adviser representatives.

notes.front: A FINRA-registered representative wants to do business with clients in a state where she has never worked. Besides federal law and FINRA rules, which laws must she consider?
notes.back: That state’s blue-sky laws, which license brokers.
notes.choices:
A) The state’s blue-sky laws
B) None: FINRA registration covers every state
C) Only the SEC’s rules
notes.choicesExplained: B: each state has its own securities laws that license brokers. C: the SEC’s rules sit alongside, not instead of, state law.
notes.explanation: Every state has its own securities laws, and they license brokerage firms and their brokers.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Blue Sky Laws”
notes.evidence: In addition to the federal securities laws, every state has its own set of securities laws—commonly referred to as "Blue Sky Laws"—that are designed to protect investors against fraudulent sales practices and activities.

notes.front: A person holds both a representative and a principal registration. What Regulatory Element content must they complete?
notes.back: Content for each representative or principal registration category they hold.
notes.explanation: Content tailored to each category is meant to give more timely and relevant training.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2021-13286 (2021-06-24), SEC notice of proposed amendments to FINRA Rules 1210 and 1240, “Transition to an Annual Regulatory Element”
notes.evidence: The proposed amendment would also require registered persons to complete Regulatory Element content for each representative or principal registration category that they hold

notes.front: What happens to a registered person who does not complete the Regulatory Element in time?
notes.back: Their registration becomes CE inactive: they may not perform, or be paid for, any activity requiring registration until it is done.
notes.explanation: If the person stays CE inactive for two consecutive years, they must requalify by examination or obtain a waiver.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2021-13286 (2021-06-24), SEC notice of proposed amendments to FINRA Rules 1210 and 1240, “Regulatory Element”
notes.evidence: A CE inactive person is prohibited from performing, or being compensated for, any activities requiring FINRA registration, including supervision.

notes.front: A representative misses the Regulatory Element deadline and becomes CE inactive. A client asks him to buy shares. What may he do?
notes.back: Not accept the order: while CE inactive he may not perform, or be paid for, any activity requiring registration.
notes.choices:
A) Refuse the order and refer the client to an active colleague
B) Take the order but waive his commission
C) Take the order, since CE inactivity only affects supervision
notes.choicesExplained: B: he may not perform any activity requiring registration, paid or not. C: inactivity covers all activities requiring registration, not only supervision.
notes.explanation: Taking an order is an activity that requires registration, so he must leave it to a registered colleague who is not CE inactive.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2021-13286 (2021-06-24), SEC notice of proposed amendments to FINRA Rules 1210 and 1240, “Regulatory Element”
notes.evidence: A CE inactive person is prohibited from performing, or being compensated for, any activities requiring FINRA registration, including supervision.

notes.front: Under Rule 1240 as amended, who must take Firm Element training?
notes.back: All registered persons, including those holding only a permissive registration.
notes.explanation: Before the change the Firm Element applied only to covered registered persons, such as those in direct contact with customers.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2021-20818 (2021-09-27), SEC order approving amendments to FINRA Rules 1210 and 1240, section II.C
notes.evidence: The proposed rule change would also amend the rule to extend the Firm Element requirement to all registered persons, including individuals who maintain solely a permissive registration

notes.front: Which existing firm training may count towards the annual Firm Element under Rule 1240 as amended?
notes.back: Training on the anti-money laundering compliance programme and on the annual compliance meeting.
notes.explanation: Once successfully completed, such training counts towards the individual’s annual Firm Element requirement.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2021-20818 (2021-09-27), SEC order approving amendments to FINRA Rules 1210 and 1240, section II.C
notes.evidence: to allow for recognition of the successful completion of existing firm training programs relating to the AML compliance program and the annual compliance meeting toward satisfying an individual's annual Firm Element requirement.

notes.front: A firm runs its own course on the structured notes it has just started selling. Which part of CE is this?
notes.back: The Firm Element, which each firm provides on the products, services and strategies it offers.
notes.choices:
A) The Firm Element
B) The Regulatory Element
C) Neither: product training is not CE
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Regulatory Element is administered by FINRA and focuses on regulatory requirements and industry standards. C: training on the firm’s products is exactly what the Firm Element covers.
notes.explanation: The Firm Element is provided by each firm and focuses on the products, services and strategies it offers.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2021-13286 (2021-06-24), SEC notice of proposed amendments to FINRA Rules 1210 and 1240, “Purpose”, (i) Background
notes.evidence: The Regulatory Element, which is administered by FINRA, focuses on regulatory requirements and industry standards, while the Firm Element is provided by each firm and focuses on securities products, services and strategies the firm offers, firm policies and industry trends.

notes.front: Rule 17a-3 requires a questionnaire or application for each associated person. What can a firm keep instead when the person’s registration was approved by FINRA or an exchange?
notes.back: A full, correct and complete copy of the applications for that registration or approval.
notes.explanation: The questionnaire must cover matters such as at least ten years of business connections and any disciplinary action taken against the person.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17a-3 (Rule 17a-3), paragraph (a), paragraph (a)(12)
notes.evidence: then retention of a full, correct, and complete copy of any and all applications for such registration or approval will be deemed to satisfy the requirements of this paragraph (a)(12)(i).

notes.front: A firm hires a representative, and a year later she leaves for another firm. Which uniform form does each event call for?
notes.back: Form U4 to register her when hired; Form U5 when her registration with the firm ends.
notes.choices:
A) Form U4 on hiring, Form U5 on leaving
B) Form U5 on hiring, Form U4 on leaving
C) Form BD for both
notes.choicesExplained: B: the forms are the other way round. C: Form BD is the broker-dealer’s own registration form.
notes.explanation: U4 is the application for registration or transfer, and U5 is the termination notice.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2010-19505 (2010-08-09), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed Rule 4530 (Reporting Requirements), “Reporting Deadline”
notes.evidence: The proposed 30-calendar-day reporting deadline also is consistent with the reporting deadline for disclosing information on the Forms BD (Uniform Application for Broker-Dealer Registration), U4 (Uniform Application for Securities Industry Registration or Transfer) and U5 (Uniform Termination Notice for Securities Industry Registration)

notes.front: Under the FINRA By-Laws, how soon must a firm file an amended Form U4 after learning of facts that require one?
notes.back: No later than 30 calendar days after learning of them.
notes.explanation: The obligation comes from Article V, Section 2(c) of the By-Laws; late disclosures can attract Late Disclosure Fees.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2014-30902 (2015-01-06), SEC order approving FINRA Rule 3110(e), section III
notes.evidence: under FINRA By-Laws, a firm is obligated to file an amended Form U4 no later than 30 calendar days after learning of the facts or circumstances giving rise for the need to file an amendment.

notes.front: A registered person learns of an unsatisfied judgment or lien against her. When must her Form U4 be amended, and does paying it off first change that?
notes.back: Within 30 calendar days of learning of it, even if she satisfies the judgment or lien before then.
notes.explanation: The duty arises on the date she receives notice or learns of the unsatisfied judgment or lien.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2014-30902 (2015-01-06), SEC order approving FINRA Rule 3110(e), footnote 50
notes.evidence: an amended Form U4 should be filed no later than 30 calendar days from that date, regardless of whether the registered person satisfies the judgment or lien in the interim period before the 30-day deadline for filing a Form U4 amendment.

notes.front: On 1 March a firm learns of facts that require it to amend a representative’s Form U4. What is the latest date for filing the amendment?
notes.back: 31 March: within 30 calendar days of learning of the facts.
notes.choices:
A) 31 March
B) At the next annual renewal
C) 30 April
notes.choicesExplained: B: amendments are due within 30 calendar days, not annually. C: the clock starts when the firm learns of the facts, not a month later.
notes.explanation: The By-Laws require an amended Form U4 no later than 30 calendar days after the firm learns of the facts.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2014-30902 (2015-01-06), SEC order approving FINRA Rule 3110(e), section III
notes.evidence: under FINRA By-Laws, a firm is obligated to file an amended Form U4 no later than 30 calendar days after learning of the facts or circumstances giving rise for the need to file an amendment.

notes.front: What does FINRA Rule 1122 prohibit?
notes.back: Filing membership or registration information that is incomplete or inaccurate so as to be misleading, or failing to correct it after notice.
notes.explanation: FINRA adopted it to make sure members and their associated persons provide complete and accurate membership and registration information.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. E9-5929 (2009-03-19), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed Rule 1122, “Purpose”
notes.evidence: the filing of membership or registration information as a Registered Representative with FINRA which is incomplete or inaccurate so as to be misleading, or which could in any way tend to mislead, or the failure to correct such filing after notice thereof

notes.front: On her Form U4 an applicant answers “no” to a question about liens, knowing a tax lien was filed against her last year. Which FINRA rule does this breach?
notes.back: Rule 1122: filing incomplete or inaccurate registration information that is misleading.
notes.choices:
A) Rule 1122
B) Rule 5220
C) No rule, if the lien is small
notes.choicesExplained: B: Rule 5220 is about honouring quotations. C: the rule has no size threshold for misleading registration information.
notes.explanation: An inaccurate answer on a registration form that could mislead is exactly what Rule 1122 prohibits.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. E9-5929 (2009-03-19), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed Rule 1122, “Purpose”
notes.evidence: no member or person associated with a member'' shall file incomplete or misleading membership or registration information.

notes.front: Under FINRA Rule 4513, how long must a member keep records of written customer complaints, and why that period?
notes.back: At least four years, to fit FINRA’s four-year routine examination cycle for certain members.
notes.explanation: The earlier requirement was three years.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2010-27495 (2010-11-01), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed books and records rules, “Records of Written Customer Complaints”
notes.evidence: To take into account FINRA's four-year routine examination cycle for certain members, the proposed rule change would require that members preserve the customer complaint records for a period of at least four years.
notes.validAsOf: 2010-11-01 · FINRA Rule 4513 as proposed in 2010; later amendments not checked

notes.front: Where must a member keep its written customer complaint records?
notes.back: At each office of supervisory jurisdiction for complaints relating to that office, or make them promptly available there when FINRA asks.
notes.explanation: This includes complaints relating to activities supervised from that office.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2010-27495 (2010-11-01), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed books and records rules, “Records of Written Customer Complaints”
notes.evidence: members may maintain the required records at the OSJ or make them promptly available at such office upon FINRA's request.
notes.validAsOf: 2010-11-01 · FINRA Rule 4513 as proposed in 2010; later amendments not checked

notes.front: A client emails a firm that her representative put her in a fund she did not approve. What must the firm record?
notes.back: A complaint record for that representative: the client’s details, date received, the complaint’s nature and how it was resolved.
notes.choices:
A) A written complaint record with those details
B) Nothing, because it arrived by email
C) Only the final outcome
notes.choicesExplained: B: a written complaint does not have to be on paper to be written. C: the record also needs the complainant’s details, the date and a description.
notes.explanation: Rule 17a-3 requires a record for each written customer complaint concerning an associated person, with the listed contents.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17a-3 (Rule 17a-3), paragraph (a), paragraph (a)(18)
notes.evidence: each written customer complaint received by the member, broker or dealer concerning that associated person. The record must include the complainant's name, address, and account number; the date the complaint was received; the name of any other associated person identified in the complaint; a description of the nature of the complaint; and the disposition of the complaint.

notes.front: Under FINRA Rule 4530(a), how soon must a firm report a specified event to FINRA?
notes.back: No later than 30 calendar days after the firm knows or should have known of it.
notes.explanation: The deadline matches the one for disclosures on the Uniform Forms, such as Forms U4 and U5.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2010-19505 (2010-08-09), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed Rule 4530 (Reporting Requirements), “Reporting Deadline”
notes.evidence: extends the time period for reporting any of the events specified in paragraph (a) of the proposed rule to no later than 30 calendar days after the firm knows or should have known of the existence of the event
notes.validAsOf: 2010-08-09 · FINRA Rule 4530 as proposed in 2010; later amendments not checked

notes.front: When is a firm excused from reporting an event under Rule 4530(a) or (b)?
notes.back: When it discloses the event on Form U5, consistent with that form’s requirements.
notes.explanation: In 2010 FINRA gave no such exception for disclosures on Forms BD and U4, though it said it would work towards removing that duplicate reporting.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2010-19505 (2010-08-09), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed Rule 4530 (Reporting Requirements), “Reporting Obligation”
notes.evidence: a firm is not required to report an event otherwise required to be reported under FINRA Rules 4530(a) or (b) if the firm discloses the event on the Form U5, consistent with the requirements of that form.
notes.validAsOf: 2010-08-09 · FINRA Rule 4530 as proposed in 2010; later amendments not checked

notes.front: On 10 June a firm learns that a regulator has made a finding against one of its representatives, an event Rule 4530(a) lists. By when must it report to FINRA?
notes.back: By 10 July: within 30 calendar days of knowing of the event.
notes.choices:
A) By 10 July
B) Within 10 business days
C) In its next quarterly statistics
notes.choicesExplained: B: 10 business days was the older deadline that Rule 4530 replaced. C: quarterly statistics cover written complaints, not event reports.
notes.explanation: Rule 4530(a) allows 30 calendar days from when the firm knows or should have known.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2010-19505 (2010-08-09), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed Rule 4530 (Reporting Requirements), “Reporting Deadline”
notes.evidence: no later than 30 calendar days after the firm knows or should have known of the existence of the event (rather than the 10 business days currently provided under NASD Rule 3070(b)).
notes.validAsOf: 2010-08-09 · FINRA Rule 4530 as proposed in 2010; later amendments not checked

notes.front: Besides specified events, what must firms report to FINRA each quarter, and what does FINRA use it for?
notes.back: Statistical and summary information on written customer complaints; it helps FINRA identify and investigate firms and people who may pose a regulatory risk.
notes.explanation: The reporting is a way of surfacing red flags: patterns that may point to regulatory risk in firms, offices or associated persons.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2010-19505 (2010-08-09), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed Rule 4530 (Reporting Requirements), “Background”
notes.evidence: require members to report to FINRA certain specified events (e.g., regulatory actions) and quarterly statistical and summary information regarding written customer complaints. FINRA uses the reported information for regulatory purposes. Among other things, the information assists FINRA to identify and investigate firms, offices and associated persons that may pose a regulatory risk.
notes.validAsOf: 2010-08-09 · FINRA Rule 4530 as proposed in 2010; later amendments not checked

notes.front: Under Rule 3270, what must a registered person give the firm before taking part in an outside business activity?
notes.back: Prior written notice, in the form the firm specifies.
notes.explanation: Passive investments and private securities transactions under Rule 3280 are exempt from this rule.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2026-19126 (2026-09-18), SEC order approving FINRA Rule 3290 (Outside Activities Requirements), section II.A.1
notes.evidence: unless he or she has provided [[Page 59260]] prior written notice to the member, in such form as specified by the member.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rules 3270 and 3280 in force; replacement Rule 3290 approved, effective date not set

notes.front: After receiving an OBA notice, what must the firm consider, and what may it then do?
notes.back: Whether the activity will interfere with the person’s duties or appear to customers as the firm’s business; it may then condition, limit or prohibit it.
notes.explanation: The firm must also decide whether the activity is really a private securities transaction under Rule 3280, and keep a record of its review.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2026-19126 (2026-09-18), SEC order approving FINRA Rule 3290 (Outside Activities Requirements), section II.A.1
notes.evidence: Based on the member's review of such factors, the member must evaluate whether to condition, limit, or prohibit a registered person's outside activity.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rules 3270 and 3280 in force; replacement Rule 3290 approved, effective date not set

notes.front: What did the SEC approve on 15 September 2026 for FINRA Rules 3270 and 3280?
notes.back: A new FINRA Rule 3290 (Outside Activities Requirements) to replace both; FINRA has yet to set its effective date.
notes.explanation: FINRA said it would choose an effective date that balances time to implement with reducing unnecessary burdens, so Rules 3270 and 3280 remain the ones to know until then.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2026-19126 (2026-09-18), SEC order approving FINRA Rule 3290 (Outside Activities Requirements), sections I and III
notes.evidence: a proposed rule change to adopt FINRA Rule 3290 (Outside Activities Requirements) to replace existing FINRA Rules 3270 (Outside Business Activities of Registered Persons) and 3280 (Private Securities Transactions of an Associated Person).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: A registered representative is invited to become a paid director of a local software company, unrelated to securities. What must he do first?
notes.back: Give his firm prior written notice under Rule 3270, in the form it specifies.
notes.choices:
A) Give his firm prior written notice
B) Nothing, because it has nothing to do with securities
C) File a Form U5
notes.choicesExplained: B: Rule 3270, still in force, covers business activity outside the firm, securities-related or not; Rule 3290 will narrow this once effective. C: Form U5 ends a registration; he is not leaving.
notes.explanation: Being a paid director of another company is an outside business activity under Rule 3270, which needs prior written notice. Once Rule 3290 takes effect, only investment-related outside activities will need notice.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2026-19126 (2026-09-18), SEC order approving FINRA Rule 3290 (Outside Activities Requirements), section II.A.1
notes.evidence: FINRA Rule 3270 prohibits a registered person from being an employee, independent contractor, sole proprietor, officer, director or partner of another person, or being compensated, or having the reasonable expectation of compensation, by any other person
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rules 3270 and 3280 in force; replacement Rule 3290 approved, effective date not set

notes.front: Under Rule 3280(b), what must an associated person’s written notice to the firm contain before a private securities transaction?
notes.back: A detailed description of the proposed transaction and their role, and whether they have received or may receive selling compensation.
notes.explanation: For a series of related transactions with no selling compensation, one written notice may be enough.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2026-19126 (2026-09-18), SEC order approving FINRA Rule 3290 (Outside Activities Requirements), section II.A.2
notes.evidence: to provide written notice to the member with which he or she is associated, describing in detail the proposed transaction and the person's proposed role therein and stating whether he or she has received or may receive selling compensation in connection with the transaction
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rules 3270 and 3280 in force; replacement Rule 3290 approved, effective date not set

notes.front: Without telling his firm, a representative sells limited partnership interests in a friend’s restaurant to three clients. What rule has he broken?
notes.back: Rule 3280: he took part in a private securities transaction without giving prior written notice.
notes.choices:
A) Rule 3280 on private securities transactions
B) Rule 3240 on borrowing
C) No rule, as the restaurant is not a broker-dealer
notes.choicesExplained: B: no loan is involved. C: the rule is about securities transactions outside the firm, whoever the issuer is.
notes.explanation: Interests in the partnership are securities sold outside the regular course of his employment, which requires written notice to the firm first.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2015-21405 (2015-08-31), SEC notice of FINRA Rule 3280, “Purpose”
notes.evidence: prior to participating in any private securities transaction, any person associated with a FINRA member must provide written [[Page 52531]] notice to the member with which he or she is associated.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rules 3270 and 3280 in force; replacement Rule 3290 approved, effective date not set

notes.front: How does the firm’s response to a PST notice differ with and without selling compensation?
notes.back: With compensation, the firm must approve or disapprove in writing; without it, the firm acknowledges in writing and may impose conditions.
notes.explanation: Selling compensation raises the firm’s involvement from acknowledgement to approval and supervision.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2015-21405 (2015-08-31), SEC notice of FINRA Rule 3280, “Purpose”
notes.evidence: If the associated person has received or may receive selling compensation, the FINRA member must advise the individual in writing whether it approves or disapproves the associated person's participation in the transaction.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rules 3270 and 3280 in force; replacement Rule 3290 approved, effective date not set

notes.front: If a firm approves a PST for which the associated person receives selling compensation, what follows?
notes.back: The transaction goes on the firm’s books and records, and the firm supervises it as if executed on its own behalf.
notes.explanation: If the firm disapproves instead, the person may not take part in the transaction in any manner, directly or indirectly.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2015-21405 (2015-08-31), SEC notice of FINRA Rule 3280, “Purpose”
notes.evidence: If the member approves the associated person's participation in the transaction, then the transaction must be recorded on the member's books and records, and the member must supervise the associated person's participation as if the transaction were executed on behalf of the member.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rules 3270 and 3280 in force; replacement Rule 3290 approved, effective date not set

notes.front: A representative tells her firm she will help a cousin’s company sell shares to investors for a 5% fee. The firm disapproves. What may she do?
notes.back: Nothing further: she may not take part in the transaction in any manner.
notes.choices:
A) Not take part at all
B) Take part if she gives up the fee
C) Take part, since she gave notice
notes.choicesExplained: B: once the firm disapproves she may not participate; giving up the fee does not undo the disapproval. C: notice alone is not enough where selling compensation is involved.
notes.explanation: A disapproved associated person may not participate in the transaction directly or indirectly.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2015-21405 (2015-08-31), SEC notice of FINRA Rule 3280, “Purpose”
notes.evidence: If the member disapproves the associated person's participation in the transaction, the associated person may not directly or indirectly participate in the transaction in any manner.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rules 3270 and 3280 in force; replacement Rule 3290 approved, effective date not set

notes.front: Under MSRB Rule G-37, when does a municipal finance professional’s contribution to an issuer official not trigger a ban?
notes.back: When it goes to an official the professional can vote for and, with their other contributions to that official, stays within $250 per election.
notes.explanation: There is no de minimis exclusion for contributions to officials the professional cannot vote for.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2015-32822 (2015-12-30), SEC notice of proposed amendments to MSRB Rule G-37, “Rule G-37 currently applies”
notes.evidence: a contribution will not trigger a ban on municipal securities business if made by an MFP to an official for whom the MFP is entitled to vote, if such contribution, together with any other contributions made by the MFP to the official, do not exceed $250 per election
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: What is the consequence under MSRB Rule G-37 of a triggering contribution to an issuer official?
notes.back: The dealer may not engage in municipal securities business with that issuer for two years.
notes.explanation: Contributions by the dealer, its municipal finance professionals, or political action committees they control can trigger it.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2015-32822 (2015-12-30), SEC notice of proposed amendments to MSRB Rule G-37, “Rule G-37 currently applies”
notes.evidence: Rule G-37(b) prohibits dealers from engaging in municipal securities business with an issuer within two years after a triggering contribution to an official of such issuer is made by

notes.front: A dealer’s municipal finance professional gives $1,000 to the campaign of a city mayor she cannot vote for. The dealer underwrites the city’s bonds. What follows?
notes.back: The contribution triggers a two-year ban on municipal securities business with that city.
notes.choices:
A) A two-year ban on business with the city
B) Nothing, as it is under $250 per election
C) Nothing, as she cannot vote for the mayor
notes.choicesExplained: B: $1,000 is over $250, and the de minimis exclusion needs her to be entitled to vote. C: not being able to vote removes the de minimis exclusion rather than helping.
notes.explanation: Only contributions to officials she can vote for, of no more than $250 per election, avoid a ban.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2015-32822 (2015-12-30), SEC notice of proposed amendments to MSRB Rule G-37, “Rule G-37 currently applies”
notes.evidence: There is no de minimis exclusion for a contribution to an official for whom an MFP is not entitled to vote.

notes.front: What is the FINRA Rule 3220 gift limit after the SEC-approved amendment?
notes.back: $300 per person per year, up from $100.
notes.explanation: The limit applies to gifts in relation to the business of the recipient’s employer.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2026-03127 (2026-02-18), SEC order approving amendments to FINRA Rule 3220, section I
notes.evidence: increase the gift limit from $100 to $300 per person per year
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: When did FINRA’s $300 gift limit take effect?
notes.back: 30 March 2026, after SEC approval on 12 February 2026.
notes.explanation: The limit had been $100 since it was set in 1992.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2026-08993 (2026-05-07), SEC notice of amendments to MSRB Rule G-20, “FINRA’s Gift Rule Amendment”
notes.evidence: FINRA's gift rule amendment, which was approved by the Commission on February 12, 2026,\23\ and became effective March 30, 2026,\24\
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: In 2026 a representative gives a client firm’s trader a $200 bottle of wine in May and a $150 gift basket in November, both in relation to the trader’s job. Is this within Rule 3220?
notes.back: No: gifts are added up per recipient over the year, and $350 exceeds the $300 limit.
notes.choices:
A) No, $350 in total exceeds $300
B) Yes, each gift is under $300
C) Yes, the limit is per gift, not per year
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the member must aggregate all gifts to a recipient over the year.
notes.explanation: Aggregation stops multiple gifts in a year to the same person from getting around the limit.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2026-03127 (2026-02-18), SEC order approving amendments to FINRA Rule 3220, section II
notes.evidence: would require that members aggregate all gifts given by the member and each associated person of the member to a particular recipient over the course of the year for purposes of ensuring compliance with the gift limit.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: Under Rule 3220.02, how must a member value tickets for sporting or other events given as gifts?
notes.back: At the higher of cost or face value.
notes.explanation: Such tickets are often bought on secondary markets at a cost different from face value, and face value is usually easy to find.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2026-03127 (2026-02-18), SEC order approving amendments to FINRA Rule 3220, section II.B.2
notes.evidence: proposed Rule 3220.02 would require that when valuing tickets for sporting or other events a member must use the higher of cost or face value.

notes.front: Which gifts fall outside Rule 3220’s limit and recordkeeping, provided their value is substantially below $300?
notes.back: Gifts of de minimis value, such as pens or notepads, and promotional items of nominal value showing the member’s logo.
notes.explanation: Examples of promotional items are umbrellas, tote bags or shirts with the firm’s logo.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2026-03127 (2026-02-18), SEC order approving amendments to FINRA Rule 3220, section II.B.6
notes.evidence: gifts of a de minimis value (e.g., pens, notepads, or modest desk ornaments) or promotional items of nominal value that display the member's logo (e.g., umbrellas, tote bags, or shirts) are not subject to the gift limit restrictions in FINRA Rule 3220(a)

notes.front: Do Rule 3220’s prohibitions generally apply to personal gifts, such as a wedding present?
notes.back: Generally not, provided the gift is not in relation to the business of the recipient’s employer.
notes.explanation: A congratulatory gift for the birth of a child is another example FINRA gives.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2026-03127 (2026-02-18), SEC order approving amendments to FINRA Rule 3220, section II.B.4
notes.evidence: Current FINRA guidance states that the prohibitions in the Gifts Rule generally do not apply to personal gifts (e.g., a wedding gift or a congratulatory gift for the birth of a child), provided that these gifts are not ``in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient.''

notes.front: What gift limit does MSRB Rule G-20 set, and why did it change in 2026?
notes.back: $300 per person per year, raised from $100 to keep G-20 aligned with FINRA’s amended Rule 3220.
notes.explanation: For dealers that are FINRA members, the change became operative on 1 June 2026.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2026-08993 (2026-05-07), SEC notice of amendments to MSRB Rule G-20, “Description of Proposed Rule Change”
notes.evidence: amend MSRB Rule G-20(d)(iv) to change the gift limit from $100 to $300
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: In October 2026 an employee of a bank dealer (a dealer that is not a FINRA member) wants to give a municipal client’s staff member a $250 gift. Which G-20 limit applies?
notes.back: The existing $100 limit, until the 1 December 2026 compliance date for bank dealers and municipal advisors.
notes.choices:
A) $100 until 1 December 2026
B) $300 since 30 March 2026
C) No limit, as it is not a FINRA member
notes.choicesExplained: B: 30 March 2026 is FINRA’s date; bank dealers keep the old G-20 limit until 1 December 2026. C: MSRB Rule G-20 applies to bank dealers.
notes.explanation: Until the 1 December 2026 compliance date, municipal advisors and bank dealers stay under the existing G-20 provisions; from that date the $300 limit applies to them too.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2026-08993 (2026-05-07), SEC notice of amendments to MSRB Rule G-20, introduction
notes.evidence: Until such compliance date for municipal advisors and bank dealers, such regulated entities would be subject to the existing provisions of MSRB Rule G-20, including, but not limited to, the gift limit (i.e., $100 limit per person per year)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: Under the non-cash compensation rules as amended in 2026, what gifts are excepted from the ban?
notes.back: Gifts of no more than $300 per individual per year that are not preconditioned on achieving a sales target.
notes.explanation: The amendment raised these limits from $100 to $300 to match FINRA Rule 3220.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2026-03127 (2026-02-18), SEC order approving amendments to FINRA Rule 3220, section II.D
notes.evidence: exceptions from this prohibition for gifts that do not exceed $100 per individual per year and are not preconditioned on the achievement of a sales target.\81\ Consistent with the proposed change to the gift limit in FINRA Rule 3220(a), the proposed rule change would raise the dollar limits in the Non-Cash Compensation Rules from $100 to $300.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: Under the non-cash compensation rules, who may pay for training or education meetings, and on what key condition?
notes.back: Offerors, generally product sponsors and their affiliates, provided the payment is not conditioned on achieving a sales target.
notes.explanation: Other specified conditions also apply to these meetings.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2020-06187 (2020-03-25), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed suitability and non-cash compensation changes, “Non-Cash Compensation”
notes.evidence: Payment or receipt by ``offerors'' (generally product sponsors and their affiliates) in connection with training or education meetings, subject to specified conditions, including that the payment of such compensation is not conditioned on achieving a sales target

notes.front: A mutual fund sponsor offers representatives a weekend at a resort, but only to those who sell $1 million of its funds this quarter. Is this allowed?
notes.back: No: non-cash compensation from the sponsor may not be preconditioned on a sales target.
notes.choices:
A) No
B) Yes, if the resort hosts some training
C) Yes, as it is not cash
notes.choicesExplained: B: training meetings paid by offerors must not be conditioned on sales targets. C: the rules restrict non-cash compensation specifically.
notes.explanation: Each permitted type of sponsor-paid non-cash compensation excludes arrangements tied to a sales target.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2020-06187 (2020-03-25), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed suitability and non-cash compensation changes, “Non-Cash Compensation”
notes.evidence: Payment or receipt by ``offerors'' (generally product sponsors and their affiliates) in connection with training or education meetings, subject to specified conditions, including that the payment of such compensation is not conditioned on achieving a sales target

notes.front: Under Rule 3220.01, is a gift handed over during a business entertainment event subject to the gift limit, and does the event’s cost count?
notes.back: Yes, the gift counts towards $300 unless personal, de minimis or promotional; the cost of the event itself does not count.
notes.explanation: FINRA stated that the value of the business entertainment event is not included in the value of the gift.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2026-03127 (2026-02-18), SEC order approving amendments to FINRA Rule 3220, section II.B.1
notes.evidence: a gift given during the course of a business entertainment event would be subject to the $300 limit on gifts in FINRA Rule 3220(a) unless it is a personal gift under proposed Rule 3220.04 or of de minimis value or a
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: A representative takes a client’s buyer to a $400-a-head dinner and, at the table, gives him a $280 watch. How much counts towards the $300 gift limit?
notes.back: $280 for the watch; the cost of the dinner itself is not included.
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the cost of the business entertainment event itself is not included in the value of a gift.
notes.explanation: Gifts during entertainment count towards the limit, but the entertainment does not.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2026-03127 (2026-02-18), SEC order approving amendments to FINRA Rule 3220, section II.B.1
notes.evidence: FINRA stated that for the purpose of this limit, the cost of the business entertainment event itself would not be included in the value of the gift.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: Which arrests or indictments must a broker-dealer’s record for each associated person include?
notes.back: Any for a felony, or for a misdemeanour relating to securities, commodities, banking, insurance or real estate, among other listed misdemeanours.
notes.explanation: Other listed misdemeanours include fraud, false statements or omissions, wrongful taking of property, bribery and forgery.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17a-3 (Rule 17a-3), paragraph (a), paragraph (a)(12)(i)(G)
notes.evidence: A record of any arrest or indictment for any felony, or any misdemeanor pertaining to securities, commodities, banking, insurance or real estate

notes.front: What are two kinds of financial public record a firm’s search to verify a Form U4 may turn up?
notes.back: Any two of: bankruptcy records; civil litigations and judgments; liens.
notes.explanation: The public records also include criminal records and business records, among others.
notes.source: Federal Register doc. 2014-23567 (2014-10-03), SEC notice of FINRA’s proposed Rule 3110(e), footnote 12
notes.evidence: Public records include, but are not limited to: general information, such as name and address of individuals; criminal records; bankruptcy records; civil litigations and judgments; liens; and business records.

notes.front: Which of these must go on the firm’s record for an associated person: (1) an arrest for misdemeanour insurance fraud; (2) a parking ticket?
notes.back: Only the arrest for misdemeanour insurance fraud.
notes.choices:
A) Only the insurance fraud arrest
B) Both
C) Neither, as both are minor
notes.choicesExplained: B: a parking ticket is not a felony or a listed misdemeanour. C: a misdemeanour relating to insurance or fraud is listed.
notes.explanation: The rule lists arrests for felonies and for misdemeanours in areas such as insurance and fraud.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17a-3 (Rule 17a-3), paragraph (a), paragraph (a)(12)(i)(G)
notes.evidence: A record of any arrest or indictment for any felony, or any misdemeanor pertaining to securities, commodities, banking, insurance or real estate

notes.front: Where does the information FINRA releases through BrokerCheck come from?
notes.back: From the Central Registration Depository, the licensing and registration system FINRA runs, fed by the uniform registration forms.
notes.explanation: Firms, associated persons and regulators report that information in answer to questions on forms such as Forms U4 and U5.
